# Noncovalent Stabilization of Radical Intermediates in the Enantioselective Hydroamination of Alkenes with Sulfonamides

**Authors:** Eve Y. Xu; Jacob Werth; Casey B. Roos; Andrew J. Bendelsmith; Matthew S. Sigman; Robert R. Knowles

**Affiliations:** †Department of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey, 08544, United States | ‡Department of Chemistry, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, Utah, 84112, United States

## Abstract

Noncovalent interactions (NCIs) are critical elements of molecular recognition in a wide variety of chemical contexts. While NCIs have been studied extensively for closed-shell molecules and ions, very little is understood about the structures and properties of NCIs involving free radical intermediates. In this report, we describe a detailed mechanistic study of an enantioselective radical hydroamination of alkenes with sulfonamides and present evidence suggesting that the basis for asymmetric induction in this process arises from attractive NCIs between a neutral sulfonamidyl radical intermediate and a chiral phosphoric acid (CPA). We describe experimental, computational, and data science-based evidence that identifies the specific radical NCIs that form the basis for enantioselectivity. Kinetic studies support that C‒N bond formation is enantioselectivity-determining. Density functional theory investigations revealed the importance of both strong H-bonding between the CPA and the N-centered radical and a network of aryl-based NCIs that serve to stabilize the favored diastereomeric transition state. The contributions of these specific aryl-based NCIs to selectivity were further confirmed through multivariate linear regression analysis by comparing measured enantioselectivity to computed descriptors. These results highlight the power of NCIs to enable high levels of enantioselectivity in the reactions involving uncharged open-shell intermediates and expand our understanding of radical-molecule interactions.

## Abstract

## INTRODUCTION

Progress in asymmetric catalysis has often relied on identifying general strategies for associating chiral catalysts with reactive intermediates.1 In recent years, extensive research efforts have focused on leveraging attractive noncovalent interactions (NCIs) between chiral catalysts and substrates to achieve high levels of enantioselectivity in polar transformations.2 More recently, extension of the noncovalent strategy to asymmetric reactions of free radical intermediates has shown significant promise with important examples demonstrated by Bach, Jiang, Phipps, Ooi, Hyster, and others.3,4 While effective, relatively little is known regarding the characteristics, energetics, and preferences of radical NCIs. In turn, this lack of understanding presents a barrier both to the further expansion of radical NCI-based strategies for asymmetric catalysis and to a more complete understanding of how these radical-molecule interactions might operate in other areas of chemistry, including redox enzymology, materials science, and supramolecular chemistry.5

To overcome this barrier, detailed molecular-level insights into radical NCIs are necessary. Leading studies from Endo, Francisco, Bietti, and others have reported on H-bonding complexes involving O-centered radicals that play key roles in atmospheric chemistry and biological systems, such as nitroxyl, peroxyl, phenoxyl, and benzyloxyl radicals.6 While important, the scope of these studies were limited in part to classes of radicals that were experimentally accessible. Advances in photoredox chemistry have enabled access to a much wider variety of radical intermediates, including N- and C-centered radicals, which have been proposed as key intermediates in catalytic asymmetric transformations.7 However, the NCIs involving most of these radical classes have yet to be examined in detail. As the energetic differences between diastereomeric transition states (TS) in asymmetric reactions are often similar to the strengths of NCIs, mechanistic investigations into enantioselective radical transformations provide unique opportunities to study open-shell NCIs.2b, 2e Yet, in the handful of reports where radical NCIs were proposed to account for high levels of enantioselectivity, few presented experimental or computational evidence supporting the role of radical NCIs in the enantiodetermining step.3a In this regard, a notable series of reports by Phipps, Goodman, and Sigman presented detailed mechanistic investigations into chiral phosphoric acid (CPA)-catalyzed Minisci reactions and revealed that the enantioselectivity is governed by a radical-molecule complex in which a CPA associates to a radical intermediate bearing a pendent H-bond acceptor.8

In recent years, our group and others have been interested in the use of proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) as a platform for developing catalytic asymmetric free radical chemistry.9 In oxidative PCET reactions, pre-equilibrium H-bonding first associates a polar protic substrate with a Brønsted base cocatalyst. Electron transfer (ET) from this H-bonded complex to an oxidant occurs in concert with proton transfer (PT) along the H-bond coordinate. These coupled exchange events result in formal bond homolysis, generating a substrate radical that is associated with the conjugate acid of the Brønsted base cocatalyst through a post-PCET H-bond.10 By kinetically coupling ET to a specific H-bonding event, PCET ensures that radical intermediates are generated exclusively as H-bonded adducts. If these post-PCET H-bonding interfaces are sufficiently stabilizing and persist on the time scale of subsequent bond-forming events, the post-PCET H-bonded complex can serve as a basis for asymmetric induction when a chiral Brønsted base cocatalyst is used. This asymmetric PCET approach has previously been demonstrated to enable high levels of enantioselectivity in reductive aza-pinacol cyclizations11 and in the oxidative activation of indoles en route to the synthesis of pyrolloindolines.12 In 2020, this manner of PCET activation was also successfully applied to the development of a highly enantioselective hydroamination of alkenes with sulfonamides (Figure 1A).13

In contrast to the two previous examples in which at least one of the H-bonding partners in the post-PCET H-bonded complex was charged, the enantiocontrol of the hydroamination was hypothesized to originate from NCIs between a neutral CPA and a neutral sulfonamidyl radical. While the high levels of enantioselectivity observed in this system suggests that there is a strong association between these two neutral species, essentially no information is available regarding the ability of sulfonamidyl radicals (or other reactive N-centered radicals) to serve as H-bond acceptors. Moreover, an extensive screen of catalysts demonstrated that incorporation of a triazole moiety into the chiral phosphate is critical for high selectivity, pointing to the possibility of a network of secondary NCIs that contribute to asymmetric induction in addition to the primary H-bonding interaction.14

Here, we report a detailed study of this asymmetric hydroamination reaction that provides insights into the key radical-molecule interactions that give rise to enantioselectivity (Figure 1C). We first present kinetic data that establishes radical C‒N bond formation as the enantiodetermining step of the catalytic cycle. We then describe a comprehensive density functional theory (DFT) investigation of the key C‒N bond forming step that elucidates the key molecular interactions that differentiate the competing diastereomeric TS structures and provides evidence for strong and stabilizing H-bonding interaction between a CPA and a reactive sulfonamidyl radical. Lastly, data science-based statistical modeling was employed to identify conserved interactions across a range of substrates and chiral phosphate cocatalysts. Taking these results together, we present a general molecular model that correlates with experimental outcomes and accounts for the key role of the aryl triazole moiety in these reactions. As such, this study represents a rare illustration of how NCIs can serve to stabilize the TS of free radical transformations and enable high levels of enantioselectivity in the reactions of highly reactive open-shell intermediates.

## RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

### Experimental Studies.

In our prior report, we proposed the following mechanism for PCET-enabled hydroamination of alkenes with sulfonamides (Figure 1B).13,15 An oxidative PCET event occurs between the excited state of an Ir photocatalyst, a BINOL-derived chiral phosphate base, and a sulfonamide substrate, leading to formal N‒H bond homolysis. The resulting sulfonamidyl radical undergoes intramolecular cyclization through addition to the pendent alkene to form a new C‒N bond and an adjacent C-centered radical. Subsequent reduction of this C-centered radical via hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) from a thiol cocatalyst then furnishes the product. Sequential electron transfer and proton transfer events (ET/PT) between the nascent thiyl radical, reduced Ir(II) photocatalyst, and the phosphoric acid regenerate the active forms of all three catalytic components.

In seeking to identify the enantioselectivity-determining step(s) of the proposed mechanism, we considered two possible scenarios: (i) enantioselectivity is determined through an irreversible C‒N bond forming step, or (ii) enantioselectivity is established during the HAT step following reversible C‒N bond formation. With regard to the latter scenario, if the HAT event is enantiodetermining, it must also be turnover-limiting. As such, these pathways should be kinetically distinguishable on the basis of the rate-dependence on thiol cocatalyst concentration.

To this end, we carried out kinetic studies with model substrate 1. First, we monitored reaction progress under standard conditions at −20 °C using 1H photoNMR spectroscopy (Figure 2A).16 While trifluorotoluene was used as the reaction solvent in the original report, deuterated dichloromethane (CD2Cl2) was used for the kinetic studies here to ensure that the reactions were fully homogeneous. During the 24-hour monitoring period, the reaction proceeded to full conversion (Figure 2B) and product 2 was obtained in 94% yield and 92% ee, which is equal to the enantioselectivity observed for the cyclization of substrate 1 in trifluorotoluene.13 The reaction displayed a first-order dependence on the concentration of substrate 1, as evidenced by a linear correlation (R2 = 0.99) in the plot of the natural logarithm of substrate concentration versus time (Figure 2C).

We then applied the method of initial rates to establish the kinetic orders for all other reaction components. Using 1H photoNMR experiments at −20 °C, the initial rates were obtained from the slopes of linear plots of [2] over time for reactions proceeding up to 10% conversion (see Supporting Information (SI) for details). As shown in Figure 3A, the initial rate of the reaction remained constant when thiol concentration was reduced from 30 mM to 15 mM. This indicates that the reaction exhibits a zeroth-order dependence on the concentration of TRIP thiol under the standard reaction conditions (Figure 3A, red), precluding the possibility of a turnover-limiting HAT step. A slight reduction in initial rate was observed at a higher thiol concentration (60 mM). This was attributed to a competitive but non-productive thiol PCET pathway that consumes excited-state PC in competition with 1 and thus lowers the rate of the productive reaction.17 The initial rate of the reaction exhibits a nonlinear dependence on the PC concentration (Figure 3B). When the PC concentration was increased from 0.5 mM to 1 mM, the initial rate increased, but then became concentration-independent at higher PC concentrations. This saturation behavior was hypothesized to result from a photon-limited regime where the concentration of the excited-state PC is bounded by the photon flux through the reaction. When the light intensity of the LED used in 1H photoNMR spectroscopy was decreased, the initial rate decreased at higher PC concentration (2 mM) but remained constant at lower PC concentration (0.5 mM) (see SI for details). These observations provide further support for a photon-limited reaction.

Interestingly, the rate-dependence on the concentration of chiral phosphate P1 was also found to exhibit nonlinear features that suggest saturation kinetics (Figure 3C). Our previous studies of similar three-component PCET systems containing an Ir photocatalyst, a phosphate base, and a H-bond donor substrate showed that the phosphate could form favorable association complexes with either the cationic Ir photocatalyst or the polar protic substrate.18 To gain insight into the bound state of P1, an NMR titration experiment in CD2Cl2 was performed in which the 31P NMR chemical shift (δ) of P1 was monitored upon the addition of various concentrations of PC or 1. The equilibrium constant K for the binding was obtained using a Benesi-Hildebrand treatment assuming a 1:1 binding stoichiometry (eq. (1)) P C / 1 Δ δ = 1 K Δ δ max + P C / 1 Δ δ max where Δ δ = δ obs – δ P 1 , and Δ δ max is the maximum value of Δ δ .19 Specifically, K, which is defined as K = slope/intercept, can be retrieved from a plot of P C / 1 / Δ δ against [PC/1]. For the binding between P1 and PC, and between P1 and 1, the obtained K values were 2.92 × 103 M−1 and 14.6 M−1, respectively (Figure S6–7).

These values are similar to related equilibria in prior reports.18b, 18c They indicate that P1 has a significantly stronger binding affinity towards PC, which could account for the saturation behavior. Along these lines, the initial rate data were also fitted to the Michaelis–Menten equation (Figure 3C, gray dotted curve) and an R2 value of 0.98 was obtained (See SI for details). The rate-dependence on P1-PC complex suggests that it may act as the active catalyst for the PCET event. Such a scenario finds support in related studies of aliphatic C‒H PCET reactions, wherein an Ir-phosphate complex was shown to act as the active abstracting species.18c

In summary, our kinetic experiments show that the reaction rate depends on 1 and the P1-PC complex but does not depend on TRIP thiol. Furthermore, we previously observed that carboamination reactions with electron deficient olefins under identical conditions in the absence of the TRIP thiol HAT cocatalyst proceeded with identical enantioselectivity.13 These findings indicate that the turnover-limiting and enantiodetermining step occurs prior to HAT. In turn, this suggests that either PCET or the C‒N bond forming step must be rate-limiting in the reaction. The PCET event involves a short-lived PC excited state (τ = 314 ns)18c and a quantum yield of 3.6% was measured for the reaction using 1H NMR actinometry (see SI for details).16b Similar N‒H PCET processes have been shown to proceed with near diffusion-limited rates and to be highly reversible.17 In light of these observations, we conclude that C‒N bond formation is the turnover-limiting step of this reaction. These results support the originally proposed mechanism (Figure 1B) and identify the C‒N bond formation to be the enantiodetermining step. Lastly, a nonlinear effect (NLE) study revealed a linear relationship between the enantiopurity of P1 and that of the product 2 (Figure S8), suggesting that only one molecule of P1 is associated with 1 during the enantiodetermining C‒N bond formation.20 This observation allowed us to focus our subsequent computational analysis on monomeric complexes of P1 and 1.

### Computational Investigations.

With this experimental framework established, we next undertook computational studies to gain a better understanding of the energetic profile of the reaction and to build a molecular model that accounts for how interactions between the chiral cocatalyst and radical intermediates give rise to selectivity.21 As the focus of this study is on the basis for enantioselectivity, we restricted our computational analysis to the key C‒N bond-forming step starting from the neutral sulfonamidyl radical 1a generated in the PCET event and ending at the generation of the neutral tertiary C-centered radical 1c. The reaction coordinate for the C‒N bond formation was constructed with (Figure 4, red) and without (Figure 4, blue) CPA PA1, which serves to model the conjugate acid of P1 generated in the PCET event. The distal octyl side chains of P1, which increase the catalyst’s solubility, were removed in PA1 to reduce computational cost. We initially considered both the sulfonamidyl nitrogen and oxygen atoms as potential H-bond acceptors. All O-bound TS structures identified were at least 3.3 kcal/mol higher in energy than the lowest energy N-bound TS (See SI for details). Therefore, we proceeded under the assumption that the N-bound pathway is the energetically favored mechanism. All relevant structures were submitted to a thorough conformational search,22 and selected geometries were optimized at B3LYP/6-31G(d)23,24 level with M06/6-311G+(d,p)/CPCM(toluene)25–27 single-point energy corrections.28,29 Only the lowest energy geometries for each structure of interest were included for analysis.30 Although B3LYP is known to possess shortcomings in describing dispersion and underestimates binding energies,31 the M06-class functionals include empirical parameters that account for dispersion effects32 and thus are used as single-point corrections in combination with B3LYP to yield more accurate binding energies in CPA-based systems.8a, 33

Moreover, despite the potential for overestimating charge transfer character, B3LYP and M06-class functionals give relatively accurate binding energies for radical-molecule complexes.34 Functionals with empirical dispersion corrections were explored, but they show significant discrepancies with the experimental values that likely result from overstabilization of the complexes (See SI for details).35

In the absence of PA1, C‒N bond formation is found to have a very low barrier of 1.94 kcal/mol, and the resulting C-centered radical 1c is 16.8 kcal/mol downhill from the TS 1b. This large energy differential between the forward and reverse steps indicates that the C‒N bond-forming process is irreversible. Nominally, achieving high enantioselectivity in a reaction with such a low kinetic barrier for the racemic background reaction would appear challenging. However, complexation between 1a and PA1 was found to be strongly stabilizing and favored by 12.4 kcal/mol. The primary attractive interaction between the two molecules is a short H-bond (1.64 Å) between the acidic proton of PA1 and the sulfonamidyl nitrogen atom (Figure 4). The spin density visualization reveals that in 1a-PA1, the spin density is localized on the nitrogen atom and the orientation of the spin density resides perpendicular to the H-bond. This analysis indicates that the H-bond acceptor is the lone pair on the nitrogen atom. The strong stabilization of 1a-PA1 suggests that this post-PCET H-bonded complex does not dissociate on the timescale of the subsequent C‒N bond-forming step, precluding the competitive racemic background reaction (Figure 4, blue).

The irreversibility of the C‒N bond formation suggests that the enantioselectivity is governed by the difference in the free energies of the TS structures (∆∆G‡). The lowest free energy barriers of activation are 0.77 kcal/mol to the major enantiomer and 2.51 kcal/mol to the minor enantiomer, with ∆∆G‡(253.2 K)calc. = 1.7 kcal/mol (94% ee). The calculated difference in TS energies agrees within error to the experimentally obtained value of ∆∆G‡(253.2 K)exp. = 1.6 kcal/mol (92% ee). For the pathway leading to the major enantiomer, the resulting CPA-bound C-centered radical 1c-PA1maj is 5.6 kcal/mol downhill from the TS 1b-PA1maj, and the dissociation of PA1 is 2.3 kcal/mol uphill to 1c. These results suggest that 1c-PA1maj has an energetic preference of 3.3 kcal/mol to undergo dissociation of PA1 prior to the HAT event. Despite having a low absolute barrier, C–N bond formation is the first irreversible step of the transformation and gates the overall reaction rate via competition with fast and non-productive back electron transfer processes that return the starting material.18b

In order to understand the molecular interactions that contribute to enantioselectivity, we further analyzed the specific NCIs present in the two competing diastereomeric TS structures (Figure 5).36 In both the major and the minor TS, we observed that PA1 and sulfonamidyl radical 1a engage in a dual H-bonding network that offers an explanation for the strength of the association and narrows the range of reactive conformations.37 The dual H-bonding network consists of a strong, primary H-bond with a distance of 1.54 Å or 1.55 Å between the acidic proton of PA1 and the sulfonamidyl nitrogen atom and a weaker H-bonding interaction with a distance of 2.33–2.52 Å between the phosphate oxo moiety of PA1 and the two aliphatic C–H bonds vicinal to the newly forming C-centered radical (Figure 5A and 5B, CPA H-bonding). Due to the radical character at the vicinal tertiary carbon, the two aliphatic C‒H bonds are likely polarized and thus are better H-bond acceptors to interact with PA1.

The main differences between the two diastereomeric TS structures arise upon examination of the interactions between 1b and the triazole and phenyl groups of PA1. In the TS leading to the major-enantiomer, the aryl group of 1b is positioned perpendicular to the triazole of PA1 in a manner that orients two aryl C‒H bonds in close contact (2.92 Å or 2.94 Å) with the π-face of the triazole ring (Figure 5A, CPA triazole). These distances are typical for C‒H-π interactions.38 The NCI isosurface between the edge of the phenyl ring and the π-face of the triazole ring offers further support for an attractive interaction. The C‒H-π interaction between these two aryl C-H bonds and the triazole stabilizes the major-enantiomer TS. The isopropyl moiety of 1b is positioned parallel to one of the terminal phenyl groups of PA1 with two alkyl C‒H bonds in proximity (3.19 Å or 3.15 Å) to the π-face of the phenyl ring (Figure 5A, CPA Ph). While these distances are slightly longer than typical C‒H-π interactions, similar distances have been observed in crystal packing39 and in protein crystal structures.40 Moreover, distinct NCI isosurfaces were observed between each C‒H bond and the π-face of the phenyl ring. This analysis suggests that these C‒H-π interactions are also points of noncovalent stabilization for the TS leading to the major enantiomer of product 2.

Conversely, in the TS leading to the minor enantiomer, the triazole of PA1 is positioned much further away from 1b, and the closest distance between the centroid of the triazole ring and the C‒H bond of 1b is 4.02 Å (Figure 5B, CPA triazole). This long distance leads to a weak triazole interaction and results in little stabilization of the minor-enantiomer TS. The phenyl groups of PA1 are oriented away from the isopropyl group of 1b and thus interact with the closer sulfonyl oxygen atoms instead (Figure 5B, CPA Ph). The C‒H bond of the triazole and three C‒H bonds of the phenyl groups are within 3 Å distance from either of the sulfonyl oxygens. These C‒H bonds act as weak H-bond donors for sulfonamide and distinct NCI isosurfaces corresponding to these H-bonds were found.41 This H-bonding network serves to stabilize the minor-enantiomer TS, thus lowering enantioselectivity. Overall, we conclude that the minor-enantiomer TS lacking the triazole-based C‒H-π interaction contains fewer significant stabilizing NCIs and is thus higher in energy. This analysis highlights the importance of the triazole ring in achieving high enantioselectivity in this transformation, which is consistent with the experimental observation that chiral phosphate cocatalysts lacking the triazole moiety gave uniformly lower selectivity (10–36% ee).13

Having formulated a plausible origin of enantioselectivity using the two diastereomeric TS structures of model substrate 1 and PA1, we sought to further explore its generality when applied to other substrates. We first tested a structurally distinct thiazole-based substrate 3 that gave comparable selectivity to model substrate 1 (Figure 6A). The computed diastereomeric TS structures for substrate 3 yield an energy difference of ∆∆G‡ = 1.8 kcal/mol (95% ee), which agrees within error to the experimentally obtained value of ∆∆G‡ = 1.7 kcal/mol (94% ee). In comparison to those of substrate 1, the two TS structures found for substrate 3 show the same relative orientation between PA1 and the substrate and preserve most of the key NCIs observed in 1 (Figure S10), suggesting the basis for enantioselectivity in these reactions is general. The main difference in the observed NCIs between 1 and 3 is that in the TS leading to the major enantiomer, in place of the attractive C‒H-π interaction between the aryl group of 1 and the triazole ring of PA1, an attractive lone-pair-π interaction with the thiazole of 3 is present. A distance of 3.37 Å is typical for lone-pair-π interactions42 and similar sulfur-π interactions are observed in protein environments where a methionine residue is in proximity (< 4 Å) to the π-face of a tryptophan residue.43 The NCI isosurface between the edge of the thiazole ring and the face of the triazole ring also supports for an attractive interaction.

We next set out to test whether our model offers an explanation for the reduction in selectivity observed for a suboptimal substrate 4, which contains a gem-dimethyl group on the carbon β to nitrogen (Figure 6B). Most NCIs found in the TS structures for substrates 1 and 3 are also present in 4 (Figure S11). The main difference presents itself in the minor TS wherein one of the methyl groups on the alkyl chain is oriented directly at the triazole group of PA1 with a C‒H bond 3.62 Å away from the centroid of the triazole ring. The closer distance between the two groups and a significantly larger NCI isosurface suggest a meaningful C‒H-π interaction here that is stronger than the interaction in the minor enantiomer TS of 1. This additional stabilization of the minor-enantiomer TS of 4 lowers its activation energy, thus leading to a reduction in selectivity. In summary, we established a TS model, which revealed that the origin of enantioselectivity arises from noncovalent stabilization of the TS leading to the major enantiomer primarily through triazole-based interaction. This TS model correctly correlates selectivity trends across three distinct substrates, providing support for the generality of the origin of enantioselectivity.

### Statistical Modeling.

To further interrogate the structural effects of the chiral phosphate and substrate on enantioselectivity, linear regression modeling was used to complement the TS analysis.45 A combination of 7 substrates and 10 chiral phosphates were used to build a dataset comprised of 40 reactions with selectivity varying from 12 to 96% ee (see SI for details). This approach allows for feature comparison across varying reaction components to understand general selectivity trends. Truncated chiral phosphates were submitted to computational analysis by initially sampling conformational space and subsequent DFT optimization of each conformer (M06-2X/def2-TZVP)25,46 to allow for extraction of descriptors for statistical modeling. The cyclized products were processed similarly as a means to simulate the active conformation of the substrates in the C‒N bond-forming TS structures. From these structures, various descriptors were collected including natural bond orbital (NBO) charges, Sterimol dimensions, and global parameters, which can be applied broadly to any molecule, such as HOMO/LUMO orbital energies and polarizability. Given the importance of NCIs in this system, we pursued specific parameters that could shed light on these key associations between various catalyst and substrate combinations.47 To accomplish this, truncated probes were constructed to mimic a key lone-pair-π interaction between the thiazole-based substrate 3 and triazole ring of PA1 (Figure 7B). The NCIs of these probes could be computed using the equilibrium distance and energies found by interpolation from single point distance scans using symmetry-adapted perturbation theory (SAPT) at the sSAPT0/jun-cc-pVDZ level.48

With this parameter library in hand,49 multivariate linear regression analysis was performed on the experimentally collected enantioselectivity data to identify features that correlate with the structure-selectivity trends. A forward stepwise algorithm was deployed and a good correlation was found (R2 = 0.85) using a three-term model including a SAPT-derived NCI parameter that describes the total interaction energy between the chiral phosphate library and the dimethyl sulfide probe, an NBO charge of the chiral phosphate, and a topological descriptor for the products (Figure 7A). Cross-validation techniques including leave-one-out (LOO = 0.80) and k-fold (k = 4, 0.80) were performed to indicate that a statistically robust model was produced.

These descriptors emphasize the importance of chiral phosphate-substrate NCIs as the interaction energy from SAPT analysis exhibits the largest catalyst parameter coefficient. This parameter carries a negative sign due to the inverse relationship between lower energy stabilization and higher selectivity. As shown in Figure 7C, the 3,5-Ph substituted phosphate catalyst significantly stabilizes the dimethyl sulfide probe relative to the mesityl-substituted catalyst resulting in an overall higher enantioselectivity range among tested substrates. Furthermore, this descriptor represents a key interaction found in the TS analysis of the system and aids in validating the proposed mechanism for asymmetric induction. Another parameter required to accurately describe the various chiral phosphates was the NBO(C5) charge on the aryl substitution of the triazole ring. The positive correlation highlights the importance of 3,5-substituted chiral phosphates that induce higher enantioselectivity by activating NCIs through the shape of the catalytic pocket. Finally, a 2D topological descriptor (PW5) was used to generalize the relative shape of the product structures by computing the atomic counts of non-hydrogen atoms along a path/walk.50 This ratio produces an overall higher score for substrate 4, capturing the detrimental effects of gem-dimethyl substitution on the newly formed, 5-membered ring. Overall, the statistical analysis has provided a complementary perspective to the TS modeling and reinforces the essential interactions observed for selectivity.

## CONCLUSION

Through this study, we established that in the PCET-enabled enantioselective hydroamination of alkenes with sulfonamides, enantiocontrol is achieved during the C‒N bond formation. DFT investigations revealed a strong neutral H-bond between the post-PCET generated sulfonamidyl radical and CPA. The diastereomeric TS structures were differentiated by a dual H-bond linkage and a network of secondary NCIs involving the triazole and phenyl group of the optimal chiral phosphate cocatalyst. The importance of triazole-participated NCIs was further validated through statistical modeling which revealed the impact of structural variations among chiral phosphates and sulfonamides on enantioselectivity. These results provided both experimental and computational evidence to support our previous hypothesis that the selectivity is dictated by NCIs between the neutral sulfonamidyl radical and CPA generated in the PCET event and reinforced the high potential for NCIs to tune selectivity in asymmetric transformations. More broadly, we anticipate that the NCIs identified in this study may serve as guiding principles for the design of future asymmetric reactions involving free radical intermediates.
